newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: New Congo revival vital for central Africa-donors.
newsitem.headline: New Congo revival vital for central Africa-donors.

text.p: International donors are ready to work with President Laurent Kabila's Democratic Republic of the Congo because its revival is crucial to the fortunes of other states in central Africa, a senior World Bank official said.

The European Union said this week it was ready to resume activities in the ex-Zaire. Other donors are rebuilding operations, despite worries about human rights under Kabila and the country's big debt arrears to multilateral agencies.
However, Jean-Louis Sarbib, one of two vice-presidents for Africa at the World Bank, told Reuters in an interview that the donors were being pragmatic.
"You really need to look for the countries that have the size and resource endowment necessary for a sub-region," he said.

"We are all not so much 'giving the benefit of doubt' to anybody, but realising that very little is going to happen in Central Africa unless we have a DRC (Democratic Republic of the Congo) that is a vibrant economy."
The various donors, grouped together as "Friends of Congo", are to meet government representatives in September or October, he said.
The focus would be on rebuilding the country and setting up, effectively from scratch, an administrative structure.

Under Mobutu Sese Seko, the dictator ousted by Kabila in May, Zaire had long given up servicing its international debt. It owed around $474 million in arrears to the African Development Bank alone at the end of 1996.

"We have gotten a lot of reassurance from the highest level that they intend to work with their creditors on a plan to manage their liabilities, their debt, in a way that will make them full partners, in good standing with the international community," Sarbib said.
He was speaking in Abidjan after a two-day meeting between senior World Bank and African Development Bank (AfDB) officials on ways of strengthening their collaboration in Africa.
He said the two organisations had already, at Congo's request, begun identifying Congo nationals living abroad who might want to return, and who had skills the country needed.

AfDB vice-president Cyril Enweze told Reuters that relations between the two banks had been excellent, even during the early 1990s when Western countries had withheld funds from the AfDB because of worries about mismanagement and arrears.
"The World Bank has always been very supportive of the AfDB and they, of all the institutions, understand our problems best," he said.
